title: Pip the Town Crier's Big Announcement
markdown:
The sun burst over Cloverbrook like a trumpet that had remembered its job. Light streamed through Asha the alpaca’s window and made her fleece look freshly invented. Her ears twitched extra. Something in the air fizzed.

Beside her, Benji the bear cub’s tummy rumbled hard enough to shiver a picture frame. “Breakfast?” He stretched. Mornings that promised berries, or honeycomb, were his favourite kind of news.

Down in the square the day was assembling itself. Birds from the oaks. Warm bread from Bartholomew Buttercream’s bakery, which made Benji rumble again. And Pip, the town crier’s son, practising a voice that wanted a bigger town. Usually he shouted Hear ye and read the simple list. Today a bigger idea buzzed like a bee with a scroll.

“Cloverbrook shall witness an announcement of unprecedented importance.” He tried the pause on an empty bench. “Prepare yourselves for news.”

Asha trotted past, ears like little dishes. “He sounds different. Vibrating.”

“He sounds like a honey pot in the square,” Benji said, already dreaming sticky.

Pip’s father, who preferred gentle tones, polished the brass bell and had already asked for shorter, not sagas. He had said it over porridge, and again by the coat pegs, and a third time while handing over the scroll as if handing over a small responsibility that might grow teeth. Pip’s imagination had other plans. He clutched the coloured paper until it crinkled like importance. “Hear ye!” The clock tower took the echo and gave it back with interest. Old Mr. Lake was winding the great clock, tick-tock as steady as a pulse, the sort of sound that makes a square remember it is a town.

“A calamitous event! Bartholomew Buttercream has almost run out of blueberry-bursting muffins!”

Heads popped from doors. A cat sat down to listen as if muffins were politics. Almost run out was not a crisis. It was a nudge to walk faster, and several people did, including a hare who had been meaning to buy one since Tuesday.

Benji: “Does almost mean one left? I could eat one left. Extra blueberries if the universe is feeling generous.”

Asha giggled. “He has made a muffin into a quest. Next he will give it a map and a dragon.”

Pip was only warming up. He swooshed the scroll; a few leaves joined the theatre. “The library’s peace has been shattered by a new book! Pages of untold tales! The cover is shockingly blue — a startling, vibrant blue that may alter the course of quiet afternoons!”

People chuckled, the warm kind that spreads without needing a leader. The librarian, who had wheeled the book out on a tidy trolley, looked proud and slightly alarmed. Mr. Lake leaned from the tower window, fond. “A flair. He can make a binding sound like weather. Cloverbrook will survive a blue cover. It may not survive the pause he is practising.”

Then the announcement Pip had been saving, voice dropped as if the cobbles were listening. “A grave disappearance! An object of immeasurable value — a missing obsidian orb — vanished! A cosmic catastrophe!”

Silence, the confused kind. An orb? Asha’s ears shot up. “A dark shiny ball.” Benji, ever practical: “Does it taste like blueberries?”

Pip pointed at the tower. “Last seen near the tallest structure!”

Mr. Lake appeared at the bottom of the steps, holding something long, black, and pointed. “This old knitting needle? Pocket all morning, next to the peppermints.”

Pip’s jaw dropped. The cosmic crisis had been wool-related. He looked at the needle, then at the tower, then at the crowd that had come because he had told them to be alarmed. Laughter moved through them, warm, not unkind, the sound of a town that likes a boy enough to let him be ridiculous in public. His face went bright. He saw, under the heat, that his big voice had actually gathered people for a shared joke, and that gathering was not nothing.

Mr. Lake patted his shoulder. “You make the ordinary sound large. That is a gift if you point it at the right ordinary. Perhaps announce arrivals instead of disasters. New books. Extra cakes. Flowers that have bothered to bloom. Grand Herald of Good News, if the title will sit still.”

Pip tasted it and found it fitted better than catastrophe. “I can do that. I will.” He took the needle, bowed to it as if it had been a worthy opponent, and handed it back.

Bartholomew, as if on cue, began handing out the last muffins from a tray that still smelled like a reason to live. Asha and Benji accepted theirs without requiring a quest; Benji’s tummy, for once, made a grateful sound instead of a forecast. Pip’s father rang the brass bell once, gently, which in their family meant well done and also shorter next time.

Pip did not try to turn the needle back into an orb. He logged muffins-almost / blue book / needle-not-orb in the crier’s book, left the scroll less epic by a third, and practised a shorter Hear ye that still had room for a pause and a grin. That afternoon he announced the blue book by its real title and the muffins by their remaining number, which was two, then one, then none, and people came anyway. Cloverbrook, fed and amused, went about a morning that no longer needed a catastrophe to feel awake.
